content: Agronomy is a specialized field within agricultural science that focuses on the study of crops and the soils in which they grow. Agronomists are dedicated to developing techniques that enhance soil utilization and increase the production of food and fiber crops. Their research encompasses a variety of areas, including crop rotation, irrigation and drainage systems, plant breeding, soil classification, soil fertility management, and weed control. Agronomy is defined as the science of utilizing plants, animals, and soils to produce food, fuel, feed, fiber, and other essential resources. Agriculture refers to the scientific, artistic, and practical discipline of farming. It involves the cultivation of soil to grow crops and the raising of animals to produce food, wool, and other agricultural products. In soil science, it is estimated that 80 to 99% of microorganisms present in soil remain unidentified. At the Arlington Agricultural Research Station, the soil is classified as Plano silt-loam. The A horizon, which is 20 cm deep, consists of silt-loam and contains 4.4% organic matter. The loess mantle at this site exceeds 1.25 meters in depth. Soil samples were collected using four 2.5-cm-diameter cores from the top 10 cm of a clover-grass pasture. These samples were immediately placed on dry ice, homogenized, and stored at -70°C for subsequent DNA extraction. Soil analysis was conducted by the Soil Testing Laboratory at the University of Wisconsin—Madison, following the methodology described by Schulte et al. The soil sample was found to contain 13% sand, 70% silt, 17% clay, 4.4% organic matter, 0.3% total nitrogen, 400 ppm of potassium (K+), and 98 ppm of phosphorus (P).5. The site is well-drained, with groundwater located more than 25 meters below the surface. The region receives an annual rainfall of 79 cm, with two-thirds of this precipitation occurring between April and October. The site experiences an average of 165 frost-free days per year.
